posts.title: The question changed from what should I post

copy.default:
I have changed the question I ask when planning LinkedIn content.

It used to be:

“What should I post?”

Now I would rather ask:

“What have we learned that deserves another test?”

That sounds like a small change, but it changes the whole content process.

A post is no longer just an isolated idea.

It can test a diagnosis.
It can test a story structure.
It can test whether a practical framework gets saved.
It can test whether a specific customer problem starts conversations.

Then the next post has a reason to exist beyond keeping the calendar full.

I still want creativity.

I just want creativity attached to evidence, so each week teaches the next one something useful.

posts.title: A full CRM can still hide a follow-up problem

copy.default:
A CRM can contain every customer and still fail to answer the useful questions.

Who is waiting for a reply?
Who enquired but never booked?
Who cancelled and still has no new appointment?
Who is genuinely due to return?
Who used to come regularly and has now gone quiet?
Who has already booked and should be excluded from follow-up?

Having the names is not the same as knowing their state.

That distinction matters because follow-up decisions depend on what is true now.

A database tells you who exists.

A useful lifecycle system should help the business understand what should happen next, who owns it, and what event means the job is finished.

posts.title: The highest-value automation might be the one that stops

copy.default:
The most valuable rule in an automation is sometimes the rule that stops it.

Customer books? Stop.
Staff member takes over? Pause.
Customer says no? Stop.
Customer opts out? Stop.
The commercial window has passed? Stop.
The person enters a different journey? Reclassify them.

It is easy to judge automation by how reliably it sends.

But reliability is not the same as relevance.

A system that keeps sending after its job is finished is not more automated.

It is less aware of the customer.

I increasingly think good lifecycle design is as much about knowing when to leave somebody alone as knowing when to follow up.

posts.title: The handoff is where good automation can become awkward

copy.default:
The awkward part of automation is often not the first message.

It is the handoff.

The system sends the acknowledgement.
A staff member replies personally.
The customer starts a real conversation.

Then the automated follow-up arrives anyway as if none of that happened.

Technically, every component worked.

Commercially, the system lost context.

A clean journey needs to know when ownership changes.

Who has the conversation now?
Should automation pause?
What event returns the person to an automated path?

The more automation a business adds, the more important those boundaries become.

The goal is not human versus automated.

It is making sure each one knows when it has the job.

posts.title: A percentage without a denominator can fool you

copy.default:
A percentage can look impressive while the evidence underneath it is tiny.

That is something I have been forcing myself to respect more in content analytics.

A high engagement rate on a very small number of impressions is interesting.

It is not automatically a winner.

The denominator matters.
The age of the post matters.
The quality of the people engaging matters.
And eventually the commercial outcome matters.

So I would rather say:

“This looks promising. Test it again.”

than:

“We cracked the algorithm.”

The same principle applies to business proof generally.

Strong evidence gets more useful when you are precise about what it does and does not prove.

posts.title: The best time to follow up depends on what happened

copy.default:
There is no universally perfect follow-up delay.

Because “follow up” can describe completely different situations.

A new enquiry that has heard nothing for a day.
A cancellation from this morning.
A no-show from yesterday.
A first-time client approaching a normal return point.
A loyal regular who is now unusually overdue.
A dormant client absent for a year.

Those moments carry different levels of intent and urgency.

So I would not start with:

“Should the delay be three days or five?”

I would start with:

“What happened, what normally happens next, and when does intervention become genuinely useful?”

Timing becomes much easier to design once the customer state is clear.

posts.title: Seven questions before I would build a recovery system

copy.default:
Before I would recommend building a Revenue Recovery system, I would want seven answers.

1. Where is the customer dropping out?
2. What evidence says the gap is real?
3. How much intent already existed?
4. Is the timing still commercially relevant?
5. Can the right people be contacted appropriately?
6. What should happen when they respond or book?
7. Is the realistic opportunity worth fixing?

Only then does the implementation become interesting.

Maybe the answer is email.
Maybe SMS.
Maybe a booking change.
Maybe a staff handoff.
Maybe no new system at all.

That is the logic behind the Revenue Recovery Check.

Diagnose the missed-revenue moment first.

Make the solution earn its place second.

posts.title: A database is not a lifecycle system

copy.default:
A customer database answers one useful question:

Who exists?

A lifecycle system has to answer several more.

What state is each customer in?
What should normally happen next?
When does action become useful?
Who owns the next step?
What should stop the journey?
What outcome should be measured?

That is why simply collecting more customer data does not automatically improve retention.

The commercial value comes from turning relevant data into better decisions about timing, ownership and the next appropriate action.

posts.title: Four Revenue Recovery states worth separating

copy.default:
Four customers can all be described as “lost revenue” while needing completely different treatment.

1. Enquired, never booked.
Intent existed, but the buying journey stalled.

2. Cancelled, not rebooked.
A booking existed, then the plan changed.

3. No-showed, unresolved.
Intent was strong enough to book, but attendance failed.

4. Previously active, now overdue.
The relationship already existed, but the normal return pattern broke.

Revenue Recovery becomes more useful when those states are separated before a message is written.

Different mechanism.
Different timing.
Different next action.

posts.title: Every automation needs an exit condition

copy.default:
Before launching an automated follow-up, define the exit condition.

The customer books.
The customer replies and a team member takes ownership.
The customer explicitly declines.
The customer opts out.
The relevant time window closes.
The customer enters a different journey.

Without exit logic, a technically successful automation can create commercially poor behaviour.

Messages keep arriving after the problem has already been solved.

A good trigger starts the right journey.

A good exit condition knows when that journey has finished.

posts.title: No-show prevention and no-show recovery use different logic

copy.default:
A reminder before an appointment and a recovery journey after a no-show solve different problems.

Before the appointment, the job is prevention.

Confirm the time.
Reduce avoidable uncertainty.
Make rearranging clear where appropriate.

After the no-show, the customer state has changed.

Now the business needs to decide whether contact is appropriate, how easy rescheduling should be, when a human should step in, and when follow-up should stop.

One workflow should not be expected to do both jobs simply because the same customer is involved.

A simple automation health check has four layers.

1. Entry
Are the right customers still entering?

2. Experience
Are the message, links, timing and next step still correct?

3. Exit
Does the journey stop or hand off when the customer state changes?

4. Outcome
Is the system producing the commercial or customer behaviour it was built for?

A green “active” toggle only answers a fifth, much narrower question:

Is the workflow switched on?

Useful automation health requires more than uptime.

posts.title: Lesson: customer states are transitions, not labels

copy.default:
Retention School: States are useful because customers move between them.

Enquired → Booked.
Booked → Attended.
Attended → Due to return.
Due → Overdue.
Cancelled → Rebooked.
No-show → Resolved.
Dormant → Reactivated.

The important part is the transition.

What event moved the person into the new state?
What job now exists?
What action should become possible?
What old action should stop?

Thinking in transitions helps automation respond to what changed instead of treating a customer label as permanent.

Retention School resource: Tear down a rebooking journey with six questions.

1. What service or behaviour creates an expected return interval?
2. When does a reminder become useful rather than premature?
3. How does the system know the customer has already rebooked?
4. What message helps without pretending urgency?
5. What happens if the customer ignores it?
6. When does the journey stop?

If those answers are unclear, writing better copy is not the first fix.

The journey logic needs to become clearer first.

posts.title: Lesson: suppression is part of the experience

copy.default:
Retention School: Suppression is not only a deliverability setting.

It is part of customer experience.

A person who has already booked should not keep receiving rebooking prompts.
A person who opted out should not re-enter through a careless workflow.
A customer in an active complaint or sensitive service state may need different treatment.
A staff-owned conversation may need automation paused.

The question is not only:

“Who can enter this sequence?”

It is also:

“Who should definitely not be in it right now?”

posts.title: Lesson: measure the outcome that matches the job

copy.default:
Retention School: The metric should match the job.

If the journey exists to recover cancellations, measure recovered bookings.

If it exists to improve rebooking, measure return behaviour in the relevant window.

If it exists to restart a dormant relationship, measure meaningful reactivation, not only opens.

Opens and clicks can help diagnose what happened inside the journey.

They are not automatically the business outcome.

Start with the job.

Then choose the metric that would tell you whether that job actually got done.

posts.title: Resource: five questions before a win-back automation

copy.default:
Retention School resource: Before automating a win-back, answer five questions.

1. What counts as dormant for this specific service or customer pattern?
2. Is there evidence the person was previously valuable or engaged?
3. What has changed since their last interaction?
4. What would make returning easier now?
5. When should the system stop trying?

“Has not purchased recently” is usually too broad to design from.

A useful win-back begins with a clearer definition of who has actually lapsed and why another contact could be relevant.
